The old lighthouse stood on a rock that the sea chewed at every day, patient as a clockmaker. Its white tower was streaked with rust and salt, and the glass room at the top held a lamp that blinked in long, deliberate sweeps. Fishermen said the light had saved more souls than the church had baptized, though they said it quietly, as if stones might hear.

At night, the keeper climbed the spiral stairs with a tin cup of tea going cold in his hand. He polished the lens, trimmed the wick, and listened to the wind press its whole body against the tower. Sometimes the foghorn sang its mournful note, and gulls rose from the cliffs like torn paper thrown into the air.

One evening, a child appeared below, holding a lantern no bigger than an apple. She asked why the light still burned when modern ships had radios and maps that spoke in blue lines. The keeper smiled. "Because," he said, "not every lost thing wants to be found by machines."

The child lifted her small lantern until it trembled in the wind. For a moment, it seemed as bright as the great beam turning overhead. The sea kept moving, the stars kept their distance, and the lighthouse continued doing what it had always done: cutting a narrow road through darkness, offering the same simple promise.

Here is land.
You are not alone.
Come home to whoever is listening, to anyone drifting, to every traveler seeking harbor tonight.
